rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed yet, so there is no evidence to exploit. The most critical first step is to establish a performance baseline that calibrates all subsequent comparisons. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space: a single modality, a single profile, and the most basic linear encoder (PCA). Running this first gives us a reference accuracy/F1 floor against which we can measure the marginal contribution of every other design axis—adding a second modality, using multiple profiles, switching to learned encoders (scvi, scgpt), or changing aggregation/fusion. Without this anchor, later experiments cannot tell us whether added complexity is genuinely helpful or merely overfitting. It is the lowest-cost, highest-information experiment to run first under a limited budget.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: The only completed experiment (config_001, rna_only + PCA) yields a low validation accuracy of ~48.5%, which is near chance for a multi-class task. This tells us almost nothing about whether the image modality carries independent signal for this task, or whether a learned RNA encoder would help. The fundamental question—does image carry discriminative information here?—is completely unanswered. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, ResNet50) establishes a clean unimodal image baseline. It changes only the modality relative to config_001 (same singleprofile, no aggregation, no fusion), isolating the effect of switching from RNA to image. 3) Why it is the best next step: Before investing budget in multimodal fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or learned encoders, we need to know whether the image channel has signal at all. If image_only performs well, multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction; if it also performs poorly, the task may require a better RNA encoder or a different representation strategy. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most consequential design axis (modality) and directly informs which of the ~50 remaining configurations are worth pursuing under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image, singleprofile, resnet50) is very weak at 20.8%. With only two data points, the highest-priority uncertainty is whether the RNA baseline can be improved, since RNA is clearly the dominant modality and most downstream multimodal configs depend on a strong RNA representation. Question tested: config_002 (RNA, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the minimal extension of config_001, isolating the effect of using multiple profiles with average-pooling aggregation while holding the encoder constant. This tells us whether the multiprofile+aggregation axis—required for nearly all multimodal configurations—adds value over a single profile. Why best next step: It is a clean, single-concept comparison to our best result, reduces uncertainty about a design axis that gates the entire multimodal search space, and if it improves on 48.5%, it validates the multiprofile direction before investing budget in more complex multimodal or encoder variants.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved the best performance so far (acc=0.591, F1=0.573), a substantial +10.6% improvement over the singleprofile baseline (config_001, acc=0.485). This confirms multiprofile aggregation is a strong design lever. However, we have no data on whether the aggregation method itself matters—avgpool is the simplest option, and a transformer could capture inter-profile interactions that pooling discards. Question: config_003 (same setup but with transformer aggregation) directly isolates the effect of aggregation method while holding modality, profile setting, and encoder fixed. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002, exploiting the strongest evidence while reducing uncertainty about a key architectural choice. If transformer aggregation helps, it validates a more expressive fusion path for later multimodal experiments; if it does not, we confirm avgpool suffices and can redirect budget toward encoder choice or multimodal fusion. Either outcome is highly informative and avoids changing multiple variables simultaneously.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) is the current best at 0.591 acc, showing multiprofile+avgpool is the strongest RNA configuration. Image (resnet50) is very weak (0.208), so the RNA representation is the dominant lever. Uncertainty: we don't yet know whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200) would improve over linear PCA in this best-known setting. This experiment (config_005) changes only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200 while holding multiprofile+avgpool fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_002. If scvi helps, it opens a new improvement axis before investing in multimodal fusion; if it doesn't, PCA is confirmed sufficient and we can redirect budget toward image encoder quality or fusion strategy. Under a limited budget, resolving whether representation learning matters is the highest-information next step.

Evidence: The best result so far is config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc. With PCA, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519, config_002 vs config_003), but that comparison was made with a simpler linear representation. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether the aggregation preference (avgpool > transformer) holds when the per-profile representation is richer (scvi_n200 latent space). Question: config_006 changes only the aggregation (avgpool → transformer) relative to the best config, isolating whether a learned attention-based aggregation can exploit the richer scvi representation to surpass simple averaging. Why best next experiment: It is the tightest single-variable comparison from the current best, directly tests an important and unresolved design decision (aggregation) in the context of the strongest encoder, and the outcome will inform whether to invest further in transformer-based aggregation or commit to avgpool for all subsequent multimodal experiments.

Evidence: scVI with multi-profile and avgpool (config_005, acc 0.650) is the best RNA-only configuration so far, and multi-profile + avgpool is the dominant setting. However, scGPT has not been tested at all, and the RNA encoder choice is a fundamental representation decision that will govern all downstream multimodal experiments. Question: config_008 (scGPT, multi-profile, avgpool) directly isolates the encoder variable against config_005 (scVI, multi-profile, avgpool), keeping profile setting and aggregation identical. This clean single-variable comparison will reveal whether scGPT's pretrained generative representation outperforms scVI's latent representation for this task. Why this is the best next step: (1) If scGPT is substantially better, it reshapes the entire multimodal search toward scGPT-based configs; if similar or worse, we can confidently lock in scVI and pivot to testing multimodal fusion or stronger image encoders. (2) It avoids the risk of prematurely investing in multimodal configs (which add two more variables: image encoder and fusion strategy) before establishing the best RNA backbone. (3) It is the highest-information experiment available: the result constrains the design of all remaining scGPT and scVI multimodal configurations, making the most of a limited budget.

The existing evidence shows a strong RNA-only baseline (scvi_n200 + multiprofile at ~0.65) but the only image-only test (config_010: resnet50, singleprofile) yielded a very weak 0.208 accuracy—essentially at chance level. This creates major uncertainty about whether the image modality contains any useful signal for this task. Config_013 (image_only, singleprofile, imagenet_vit_l) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_010, isolating the effect of a much stronger pretrained image encoder (ViT-L vs ResNet50). If ViT-L substantially improves image-only performance, it justifies investing remaining budget in multimodal fusion experiments. If it remains near chance, it strongly suggests image features are not informative for this task, allowing us to redirect budget toward refining the RNA pipeline (e.g., scgpt+transformer, or singleprofile scvi_n200) rather than exploring 30+ multimodal configurations that would likely underperform the 0.65 RNA baseline. This is the highest-uncertainty-reduction experiment available under the limited budget.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile is the strongest configuration (~0.65 acc), while image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23 acc for both resnet50 and ViT-L). The critical open question is whether fusing the weak image signal with the strong RNA signal yields any complementary benefit, or whether it merely adds noise. This experiment (config_030: multimodal, scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) is the most direct logical extension of the best RNA-only result, adding the simplest image encoder (resnet50, already characterized) and simplest fusion (concat). It isolates the single question 'does image add value when combined with the best RNA representation?' without confounding changes to encoder, aggregation, or fusion strategy. If it fails to exceed 0.65, it strongly argues against pursuing multimodal configurations and redirects budget to RNA-only refinements; if it succeeds, it justifies further fusion and image-encoder exploration.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile+avgpool is the best RNA-only model (0.6501 acc, config_005). The sole multimodal experiment (config_030: scvi_n200 + resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) scored 0.6315, actually worse than RNA-only, suggesting concat fusion with a weak image encoder (~0.21 alone) introduces noise. Image-only models are very weak (0.21–0.23), so the image signal is marginal. Question: Does weighted fusion allow the model to downweight the noisy image channel and recover (or exceed) RNA-only performance? This is a minimal change from config_030 (only concat→weighted), isolating the fusion mechanism. Why best next experiment: It directly diagnoses whether the multimodal underperformance is a fusion artifact or a fundamental lack of complementary image information. If weighted recovers to ~0.65, the image adds no value but is harmless; if it exceeds 0.65, there is hidden complementary signal; if it stays at ~0.63, the image is actively harmful regardless of fusion. This single result sharply narrows the remaining multimodal search space and is more informative than swapping the image encoder (which is weak either way) or testing transformer aggregation (already shown ≈ avgpool for scvi_n200).
